questions.q: Given {"user": {"address": {"city": "London"}}}, what does user.address.city evaluate to?
options: An error, since nesting three levels isn't allowed
questions.explain: Each dot steps into an object by key — user, then address, then city — landing on the string "London".

questions.q: Given {"orders": [{"id": 1001}, {"id": 1002}]}, what does orders[1].id evaluate to?
options: An error, since arrays can't contain objects
questions.explain: orders[1] steps into the array at position 1 (the second item, zero-indexed), and .id reads that object's id field: 1002.

questions.q: In dot/bracket path notation, what's the difference between a "." step and a "[n]" step?
options: There is no difference; they're interchangeable
A "[n]" step only works on strings
A "." step accesses an object by key; a "[n]" step accesses an array by numeric position
A "." step is only valid for numbers
questions.explain: Dot notation steps into an object using a key name; bracket notation steps into an array using a zero-based numeric index.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say AI provider API responses are a good real-world example of nested JSON?
options: Because nesting only applies to request bodies, never responses
Because AI provider responses are always flat with no nesting
Because a response like content[0].text uses the exact array-index-then-key pattern this lesson teaches
Because AI providers don't use JSON at all
questions.explain: An AI provider's response typically nests a content array whose items are objects with their own fields (like text) — directly matching the path-reading pattern this lesson covers.
